Above the drowned continent, the cloud learned to think by carrying the evaporated breath of cities. It drifted until magnetic storms uncovered a library on a mountain whose name no map remembered. The roof had folded inward, yet the stacks remained dry, sealed by glass older than the last republic. The cloud seeped through cracks and read without eyes, tasting ink, dust, fingerprints, pollen, marginal notes, and the salt left by hands that had turned pages before the sea rose.

It found histories praising conquest, recipes for vanished fruit, children’s drawings of animals extinct before the children grew old. Each absorbed fact made the cloud heavier. Rain gathered inside it, but falling would blur the books. So it learned restraint, hovering season after season, shading the library from sun, feeding moss but sparing paper.

Centuries later, seedlings rooted in the reading room. Their leaves lifted words into green veins. When wind shook them, they whispered fragments across the empty world. The cloud understood then: memory kept untouched becomes a tomb; memory shared becomes weather, returning. Beneath them, dormant machines woke, misted lenses shining, and copied each whisper into crystal seeds for travelers who might someday return from far shores again.
